exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with symmetric hand swelling and morning stiffness >2 hours – what clinical features differentiate rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis? — Look for small‑joint symmetric swelling, prolonged morning stiffness, systemic symptoms; osteoarthritis shows distal joint involvement, crepitus, no systemic signs.

A patient with HIV presents with mono‑articular knee pain and fever – what is your immediate management? — Perform urgent joint aspiration, send for Gram stain and culture, start empirical antibiotics after samples; avoid steroids until infection ruled out.

You have a limited lab set; how would you confirm rheumatoid arthritis? — Use clinical 2010 ACR/EULAR criteria (joint count, duration, serology if available, acute‑phase reactants, radiographs) and start DMARD based on high disease activity.

A young man with low‑back pain, enthesitis and reduced chest expansion – which red flag prompts urgent referral? — Suspect spinal cord compression or severe ankylosing spondylitis; arrange urgent MRI and rheumatology input.

Why is methotrexate preferred over long‑term NSAIDs in rheumatoid arthritis? — Methotrexate modifies disease course and prevents joint damage, whereas NSAIDs only relieve pain and have gastrointestinal/renal toxicity with chronic use.
In a patient with lupus and proteinuria, why would you avoid high‑dose NSAIDs? — NSAIDs can worsen renal function and precipitate hypertension; renal‑protective agents and steroids are safer.
How does the DAS28 score influence treatment decisions? — Scores >5.1 indicate high disease activity, prompting escalation to biologic DMARDs; ≤2.6 suggests remission, allowing tapering.
What laboratory result could mislead you in early septic arthritis and how to overcome it? — A normal white‑cell count; repeat aspiration or rely on clinical signs and imaging if suspicion remains.

ai.summary: Rheumatologic diseases present with joint, muscle and systemic inflammation. In low‑resource African settings infections, HIV and endemic parasites are common triggers. Clinical reasoning focuses on pattern recognition, limited investigations and timely treatment.

sections.p: Rheumatology covers disorders that cause inflammation, pain or deformity of joints, muscles, tendons and related organs. Diagnosis relies on history, pattern of joint involvement and basic labs.

t.b: Is the effusion inflammatory, septic or crystal‑induced? Positive Gram stain or high neutrophils (>50 % polymorphs) suggests infection; needle‑shaped crystals point to gout.
Do they support rheumatoid arthritis? Positive anti‑CCP is highly specific; RF may be positive in infections or hepatitis.
Are inflammatory markers elevated? Helps gauge activity but can be normal in early disease.

3.2 < DAS28 ≤5.1 = moderate activity
DAS28 >5.1 = high activity
sections.p: Severity guides treatment intensity. For rheumatoid arthritis, the DAS28 score (tender + swollen joint count, ESR/CRP, patient global) categorises remission, low, moderate or high disease activity.

sections.p: Recognise features that demand urgent action.

b: Infection‑related arthritis – appropriate antimicrobial therapy; avoid steroids until infection cleared
Rheumatoid arthritis – start disease‑modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) such as methotrexate; add low‑dose prednisolone for bridge therapy
SLE – hydroxychloroquine first line; add steroids for organ involvement, avoid NSAIDs if renal disease present
Ankylosing spondylitis – NSAID (e.g., ibuprofen) as first line; consider physiotherapy; avoid long‑term steroids
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control inflammation and prevent damage.

b: Assess disease activity every 3 months with DAS28 or clinical score
Screen for drug toxicity: liver function for methotrexate, renal function for NSAIDs
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus; give TB prophylaxis if indicated
Educate on joint protection and early physiotherapy
Septic vs. crystal arthritis – aspiration and Gram stain are decisive
Rheumatoid vs. osteoarthritis – rheumatoid has morning stiffness, symmetrical small‑joint swelling; osteoarthritis shows crepitus and distal joint involvement
Lupus vs. rheumatoid arthritis – lupus has malar rash, renal involvement, anti‑dsDNA positivity
RF can be negative early in rheumatoid arthritis; rely on clinical pattern
ESR may be normal in early lupus flares; check complement levels if suspicion remains
Joint aspiration may be dry in early septic arthritis; repeat if clinical suspicion persists
sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or non‑specific findings.

whenToSeekHelp: Septic arthritis – severe pain, fever, inability to bear weight
Rapidly progressive neurological deficit in ankylosing spondylitis
Acute renal failure or pulmonary hemorrhage in lupus
